- D: Rule 1.13(c) does permit reporting out in some circumstances, regardless of Rule 1.6; it is unavailable here only because of Rule 1.13(d).
- E: Rule 1.13(d) applies to defense and investigation counsel whatever the timing; the limit here is the role, not whether the fraud continues.
Rule: Rule 1.13(c) permits reporting out (regardless of Rule 1.6) if the highest authority fails to address a clear violation of law reasonably certain to cause substantial injury to the organization; Rule 1.13(d) excludes lawyers hired to investigate or defend the alleged violation.

## Final 1 · Q77 · Pro Bono, Appointments, and Public-Service Organizations (MR 6.1–6.5) — MR 6.2: court appointment and good cause
A judge appoints Lawyer Sid to represent an indigent defendant charged with assaulting a police officer. Sid, a former officer, asks to be excused because he dislikes defendants who hurt police, though he admits he could represent the defendant competently and his feelings wouldn't affect his work. Is Sid's reason good cause to avoid the appointment?

A. Yes, because a lawyer may always decline a matter he finds distasteful.
B. Yes, because Sid's former employment creates a nonconsentable conflict of interest.
C. No, because a lawyer must accept every court appointment, whatever the reason for declining.
D. No, because his dislike won't impair his representation of the client.
E. Yes, if Sid instead agrees to do 50 hours of other pro bono work this year.

Answer: D
- A: A lawyer can usually decline private matters, but Rule 6.2 limits avoiding court appointments to good cause.
- B: Past police work, without more, doesn't create a Rule 1.7 conflict that prevents him from representing the defendant.
- C: Rule 6.2 does recognize good cause, including repugnance strong enough to impair the representation.
- D: Correct. Rule 6.2 says a lawyer shall not seek to avoid an appointment except for good cause, such as when (a) it would violate the Rules or other law, (b) it would be an unreasonable financial burden, or (c) the client or cause is so repugnant to the lawyer as to be likely to impair the relationship or the lawyer's ability to represent the client. Sid admits his feelings won't affect his work.
- E: Rule 6.1's aspirational pro bono goal isn't a substitute for an appointment; Rule 6.2 asks only whether good cause exists.
Rule: Rule 6.2: don't seek to avoid an appointment except for good cause (any one suffices): (a) it would violate the Rules or other law, (b) unreasonable financial burden, or (c) the client or cause is so repugnant as to be likely to impair the relationship or representation.

## Final 1 · Q78 · Truthfulness in Statements to Others (MR 4.1) — MR 4.1(a), Comment [2]: negotiation statements
Lawyer Tad represents a buyer negotiating to purchase a small business. Which of the following statements by Tad to the seller's lawyer would most likely violate Rule 4.1?

A. "My client has an accountant's report showing the business lost money last year," when no such report exists.
B. "My client won't pay a penny more than $400,000," when the client has authorized up to $450,000.
C. "Frankly, this business isn't worth anything close to your asking price."
D. "My client is looking at several other businesses," when the client has looked at two.
E. "We think your client's projections are optimistic," when Tad privately thinks they're reasonable.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. Rule 4.1(a) forbids knowingly making a false statement of material fact or law to a third person. Inventing a document is a false statement of fact, not negotiation puffery.
- B: Rule 4.1, Comment [2] says a party's intentions as to an acceptable settlement of a claim are ordinarily not taken as statements of material fact under generally accepted negotiation conventions.
- C: Estimates of price or value are, under Comment [2], ordinarily not statements of material fact.
- D: This is true, so it isn't a false statement at all; a lawyer need not volunteer how serious the other options are.
- E: An opinion about projections in a negotiation is the kind of posturing that Comment [2] doesn't treat as a statement of material fact.
Rule: Rule 4.1(a) bars knowingly false statements of material fact or law to third persons; under Comment [2], estimates of price or value and a party's settlement intentions are ordinarily not material facts, but invented facts or documents are.

## Final 1 · Q79 · Truthfulness in Statements to Others (MR 4.1) — MR 4.1(b) defers to MR 1.6
Lawyer Uma represents a seller of a house. During negotiations, Uma learns from her client, in confidence, that the basement floods every spring. The buyer hasn't asked about flooding. State law imposes no duty on a seller to disclose it, and the client hasn't used Uma's services to make any misrepresentation. Must Uma disclose the flooding to the buyer?

A. Yes, because a lawyer must disclose every material fact that the other side would want to know.
B. Yes, because failing to disclose a known defect is always a false statement under Rule 4.1(a).
C. No, because a lawyer never has a duty to disclose anything to a third person.
D. Yes, but only after withdrawing, so that the disclosure isn't made while she represents the seller.
E. No, because the client hasn't committed a fraud through Uma, and Rule 1.6 protects the information.

Answer: E
- A: Rule 4.1, Comment [1] says a lawyer generally has no affirmative duty to inform an opposing party of relevant facts.
- B: Silence isn't a false statement unless it amounts to a misrepresentation, such as a half-truth; Uma has said nothing about flooding.
- C: Too broad. Rule 4.1(b) imposes a duty in narrow circumstances, and a lawyer can't make misleading partial statements.
- D: Withdrawal doesn't create a duty to disclose confidential information; Rule 1.6 continues to protect it.
- E: Correct. Rule 4.1(b) requires disclosure of a material fact only when necessary to avoid assisting a client's criminal or fraudulent act, and then only if Rule 1.6 doesn't prohibit it. No fraud is involved on these facts, and Rule 1.6(a) protects the information.
Rule: Rule 4.1(b) requires disclosure of a material fact only when necessary to avoid assisting a client's crime or fraud, and only if Rule 1.6 permits; otherwise a lawyer has no general duty to volunteer facts, but must not make misleading half-truths.

## Final 1 · Q80 · Represented Persons: The No-Contact Rule (MR 4.2) — MR 4.2: represented person initiates contact
Lawyer Vic represents a homeowner suing a contractor, Wes, who is represented by counsel. Wes calls Vic directly, says his own lawyer is "useless," and asks to talk about settling. Wes says he consents to talking without his lawyer. May Vic discuss settlement with Wes?

A. Yes, because Wes initiated the call and consented to speaking without his lawyer.
B. Yes, so long as Vic tells Wes that he represents the homeowner and not Wes.
C. Yes, if Vic limits the conversation to settlement and avoids discussing the merits.
D. No, because the contact needs the consent of Wes's lawyer.
E. No, unless Vic first obtains a court order permitting the contact.

Answer: D
- A: The protected person's consent isn't enough; only the other lawyer's consent (or law or court order) authorizes the contact (Rule 4.2, Comment [3]).
- B: Clarifying one's role is the rule for unrepresented persons under Rule 4.3; Wes is represented.
- C: Settlement is part of "the subject of the representation"; Rule 4.2 bars the contact entirely.
- D: Correct. Rule 4.2 forbids communicating about the subject of the representation with a person the lawyer knows is represented in the matter "unless the lawyer has the consent of the other lawyer." Rule 4.2, Comment [3] says the Rule applies even if the represented person initiates or consents to the communication.
- E: A court order is one route, but the ordinary one is the other lawyer's consent. The choice isn't limited to a court order.
Rule: Rule 4.2: in representing a client, don't communicate about the matter with a person you know is represented in it unless that person's lawyer consents or law or a court order authorizes it; the represented person's own consent or initiation doesn't matter (Comment [3]), but the parties may talk to each other directly (Comment [4]).

## Final 1 · Q81 · Represented Persons: The No-Contact Rule (MR 4.2) — MR 4.2, Comment [7]: organizational constituents
Lawyer Xo represents an employee suing Yarrow Corp., which is represented by counsel, for workplace injuries. Xo wants to interview, without Yarrow's lawyer present, (1) the plant manager whose orders allegedly caused the injury and (2) a former maintenance worker who left Yarrow last year and saw the accident. Which interviews does Rule 4.2 forbid without Yarrow's counsel's consent?

A. Both interviews, because both people have information about the accident.
B. The interview with the plant manager only.
C. The interview with the former worker only, because he is no longer protected by Yarrow's counsel.
D. Neither interview, because only Yarrow's officers and directors are protected by Rule 4.2.
E. Neither interview, if Xo identifies herself and her client at the start.

Answer: B
- A: Rule 4.2 doesn't protect every employee with information, and Comment [7] says it doesn't reach former constituents.
- B: Correct. Rule 4.2, Comment [7] protects a current constituent who supervises, directs or regularly consults with the organization's lawyer about the matter, has authority to obligate the organization, or whose act or omission may be imputed to it. The manager's orders may be imputed to Yarrow. Consent of the organization's lawyer is not required for a former constituent.
- C: This reverses the rule: the current manager is protected, and the former worker isn't.
- D: Comment [7] reaches beyond officers to any constituent whose act or omission may be imputed to the organization, such as this manager.
- E: Identifying herself is what Rule 4.3 requires with unrepresented persons; it doesn't permit contact with a represented organization's protected constituent under Rule 4.2.
Rule: For a represented organization, Rule 4.2, Comment [7] protects current constituents who supervise, direct or regularly consult with its lawyer about the matter, can obligate it, or whose conduct may be imputed to it; former constituents may be contacted, though the lawyer must not seek privileged information (Rule 4.4(a)).

## Final 1 · Q82 · Unrepresented Persons (MR 4.3, 3.4(f)) — MR 4.3: legal advice to an unrepresented person
Lawyer Zane represents a landlord in a dispute with a tenant, Ana, who has no lawyer. Ana calls Zane and asks whether she has any legal defense to the landlord's claim for back rent. Which response is proper?

A. "Legally, you don't have any defense, so you should just pay what you owe."
B. "I'm a neutral lawyer handling this dispute, and I'll try to be fair to both of you."
C. "I represent your landlord, so I can't advise you; you may want your own lawyer."
D. "You might have a defense based on the landlord's failure to make repairs, but I can't say more."
E. "I can't talk to you at all unless your lawyer is on the line."

Answer: C
- A: That is legal advice to a person whose interests conflict with Zane's client's, which Rule 4.3 forbids.
- B: Rule 4.3 forbids stating or implying that the lawyer is disinterested.
- C: Correct. Rule 4.3 forbids giving legal advice to an unrepresented person, other than the advice to secure counsel, when the lawyer knows or reasonably should know that the person's interests conflict or may conflict with the client's. Zane must also make clear he isn't disinterested.
- D: Even a partial suggestion about a defense is legal advice, and pointing out a defense to the client's opponent is also inconsistent with Zane's duties to his client.
- E: Ana has no lawyer, so Rule 4.2 doesn't apply; Zane may talk to her, negotiate, and state his client's position, so long as he complies with Rule 4.3.
Rule: Rule 4.3: when dealing with an unrepresented person, don't state or imply disinterest, correct misunderstandings of your role, and give no legal advice (other than to get a lawyer) if interests conflict or may conflict; stating facts or your client's position is permitted.

## Final 1 · Q83 · Involvement in a Client's Wrongdoing (MR 1.2(d)) — MR 1.2(d): advising on consequences vs. assisting
Client Bo, a restaurant owner, asks Lawyer Cal how much he could save by paying his cooks in cash "off the books" and what the penalties would be if the state labor department found out. Which response by Cal is proper?

A. Help Bo set up a cash payroll, so long as Cal advises him that it is illegal.
B. Refuse to discuss the subject at all, because discussing illegal conduct is assisting it.
C. Explain the legal consequences, including penalties, but decline to help set it up.
D. Tell Bo how to keep the labor department from discovering the cash payments.
E. Report Bo to the labor department, because he has disclosed a plan to commit a crime.

Answer: C
- A: Advising that it's illegal doesn't permit assisting; setting up the payroll is assisting in conduct Cal knows is unlawful, which Rule 1.2(d) forbids.
- B: Rule 1.2(d) expressly permits discussing the legal consequences of a proposed course of conduct.
- C: Correct. Rule 1.2(d) forbids counseling or assisting a client in conduct the lawyer knows is criminal or fraudulent, but lets the lawyer "discuss the legal consequences of any proposed course of conduct with a client." Explaining the penalties is proper; helping Bo carry out the scheme is not.
- D: Advice on avoiding detection is counseling the client to break the law, forbidden by Rule 1.2(d).
- E: No Rule 1.6(b) exception applies to a plan that hasn't used Cal's services; disclosure would violate Rule 1.6(a).
Rule: Rule 1.2(d): don't counsel or assist a client in conduct you know is criminal or fraudulent, but you may discuss the legal consequences of any proposed course of conduct and help the client test the law in good faith (Comment [12]).

## Final 1 · Q84 · Involvement in a Client's Wrongdoing (MR 1.2(d)) — MR 1.16(a)(4): client persists in using the lawyer's services
Lawyer Dee is helping Client Eve with loan applications. Dee discovers that Eve has been inflating her income figures on the forms Dee prepares. Dee explains that she can't help with false applications and why, but Eve insists on submitting the inflated figures through Dee. Under the current Model Rules, what must Dee do?

A. Continue the representation, but remove her own name from the applications.
B. Withdraw only if she reasonably believes the fraud will cause substantial financial injury to the lender.
C. Report Eve to the lender, because a lawyer must disclose a client's fraud.
D. Continue, because a lawyer may withdraw for a client's fraud but is never required to.
E. Withdraw, because Eve persists in using her services to commit fraud.

Answer: E
- A: Continuing while the client uses her work to commit fraud is assisting fraud under Rule 1.2(d), and Rule 1.16(a)(4) requires withdrawal.
- B: The withdrawal duty in Rule 1.16(a)(4) doesn't depend on the amount of injury; the "substantial injury" language belongs to the disclosure exceptions in Rule 1.6(b)(2)–(3).
- C: Rule 1.6(b)(2) may permit disclosure where the client used the lawyer's services, but it doesn't require it; the mandatory duty here is withdrawal.
- D: Permissive withdrawal is Rule 1.16(b)(2)–(3); Rule 1.16(a)(4) makes withdrawal mandatory when the client persists after the lawyer's warning.
- E: Correct. Rule 1.16(a)(4), added in 2023, requires a lawyer to withdraw when the client "seeks to use or persists in using the lawyer's services to commit or further a crime or fraud, despite the lawyer's discussion pursuant to Rules 1.2(d) and 1.4(a)(5)." Continuing would also violate Rule 1.2(d).
Rule: If a client seeks to use or persists in using the lawyer's services to commit a crime or fraud after the lawyer explains the limits (Rules 1.2(d), 1.4(a)(5)), the lawyer must decline or withdraw under Rule 1.16(a)(4); the lawyer may also consider disclosure under Rule 1.6(b)(2)–(3).

## Final 1 · Q85 · Abusive Tactics, Threats, and Reporting Misconduct (MR 4.4(a), 8.3) — MR 8.3(a), (c): reporting another lawyer
Lawyer Fin learns from opposing counsel's own email, sent to Fin by mistake, that opposing counsel has been taking money from a client trust account to pay office rent. Fin's own client didn't give him this information, and it doesn't relate to Fin's representation of his client. Must Fin report opposing counsel?

A. No, because Fin learned of the conduct through an inadvertently sent email.
B. No, because a lawyer is required to report only misconduct he has personally witnessed.
C. Yes, because he knows of a violation that raises a substantial question about the lawyer's honesty and fitness.
D. Yes, but only after first confronting opposing counsel and giving him a chance to repay the money.
E. No, because the duty to report applies only to lawyers in the reporting lawyer's own firm.

Answer: C
- A: How Fin learned of it doesn't excuse the reporting duty; Rule 4.4(b) requires notice to the sender, but Rule 8.3(a) still applies.
- B: Rule 8.3(a) turns on knowledge, which can come from any source, not personal observation.
- C: Correct. Rule 8.3(a) requires a lawyer who knows that another lawyer has committed a violation of the Rules raising a substantial question as to that lawyer's honesty, trustworthiness or fitness to inform the appropriate professional authority. Misusing trust funds plainly qualifies. Fin should also notify the sender under Rule 4.4(b).
- D: Rule 8.3(a) doesn't require confronting the other lawyer first or giving a chance to cure.
- E: Rule 8.3(a) applies to "another lawyer," whether or not in the same firm.
Rule: Rule 8.3(a): a lawyer who knows another lawyer committed a violation raising a substantial question as to honesty, trustworthiness or fitness must inform the appropriate professional authority; Rule 8.3(c) excepts information protected by Rule 1.6 and information gained in an approved lawyers assistance program.

## Final 1 · Q86 · Abusive Tactics, Threats, and Reporting Misconduct (MR 4.4(a), 8.3) — MR 4.4(a): no substantial purpose other than to burden
Lawyer Gil represents a defendant in a minor contract case. To pressure the plaintiff, Gil schedules the plaintiff's elderly mother, who has no knowledge of the dispute, for a full-day deposition in a city three hours from her home, and serves subpoenas on the plaintiff's employer for records that have nothing to do with the case. Is Gil subject to discipline?

A. No, because a lawyer may use any discovery the rules of civil procedure permit.
B. No, because Rule 4.4(a) protects only parties to the case, not their relatives or employers.
C. Yes, but only if a court first sanctions Gil for the discovery.
D. Yes, because he used means that have no substantial purpose other than to burden third persons.
E. No, because aggressive tactics are part of zealous advocacy for a client.

Answer: D
- A: Discovery that is permitted on its face still violates Rule 4.4(a) when its only substantial purpose is to burden third persons.
- B: Rule 4.4(a) protects "third persons," which includes non-party witnesses and businesses.
- C: Discipline doesn't depend on a court sanction; the two are independent.
- D: Correct. Rule 4.4(a) forbids a lawyer, in representing a client, to "use means that have no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay, or burden a third person." The mother and the employer are third persons, and the discovery serves no legitimate purpose. Rule 3.4(d) and court sanctions may apply too.
- E: Zeal doesn't excuse tactics with no substantial purpose other than to burden others (Rule 4.4(a)).
Rule: Rule 4.4(a): don't use means with no substantial purpose other than to embarrass, delay or burden a third person, or methods of obtaining evidence that violate a person's legal rights; the same conduct may draw sanctions under FRCP 11, FRCP 26(g) or 28 U.S.C. § 1927.

## Final 1 · Q87 · Restricting Future Practice (MR 5.6) — MR 5.6(b): settlement restricting practice
Lawyer Hoyt represents ten tenants suing a landlord over mold. The landlord offers a generous settlement on the condition that Hoyt agree never to represent any other tenant against the landlord. The tenants want Hoyt to accept. May Hoyt agree to the condition?

A. Yes, because the clients want the settlement and the decision to settle is theirs.
B. No, because he may not agree to a practice restriction in a settlement.
C. Yes, if the restriction is limited to a reasonable time and geographic area.
D. No, but the landlord's lawyer commits no violation by proposing it.
E. Yes, so long as Hoyt doesn't represent any other tenants against the landlord.

Answer: B
- A: The clients decide whether to settle, but Rule 5.6(b) forbids the lawyer from agreeing to this term even with their consent.
- B: Correct. Rule 5.6(b) forbids a lawyer to participate in offering or making "an agreement in which a restriction on the lawyer's right to practice is part of the settlement of a client controversy." Rule 5.6, Comment [2] confirms that the Rule bars agreeing not to represent other persons as part of settling a client's claim; like the restrictions in Rule 5.6(a) (Comment [1]), such terms limit future clients' freedom to choose a lawyer.
- C: Reasonableness limits apply in some contexts, but Rule 5.6(b) bars any practice restriction as part of a settlement.
- D: Rule 5.6(b) bars participating "in offering or making" the agreement, so the landlord's lawyer who proposes it violates the Rule too.
- E: Complying with the restriction doesn't make the agreement permissible.
Rule: Rule 5.6: no agreement restricting a lawyer's right to practice (a) after leaving a firm or job (except retirement-benefit conditions) or (b) as part of settling a client controversy; both the offering and accepting lawyers violate Rule 5.6(b).

## Final 1 · Q88 · Advertising and Solicitation (MR 7.1–7.3, 7.6) — MR 7.3(b): live solicitation for pecuniary gain
After a highway pileup, Lawyer Ivy goes to the hospital and approaches injured drivers in the emergency waiting room, offering to represent them on a contingent fee. One of the drivers is Ivy's college roommate. Is Ivy subject to discipline?

A. No, because she is offering truthful information about legal rights to people who need it.
B. Yes, as to every driver she approached, including her roommate.
C. No, because a contingent fee means she charges nothing unless the drivers recover.
D. No, unless one of the drivers had told her he didn't want to be solicited.
E. Yes, as to the strangers, because live solicitation for pecuniary gain is barred.

Answer: E
- A: Truthfulness doesn't save in-person solicitation for pecuniary gain; Rule 7.3(b) bars it because of the risk of undue influence.
- B: Rule 7.3(b)(2) exempts persons with a family, close personal, or prior business or professional relationship with the lawyer.
- C: A contingent fee is still pecuniary gain; Rule 7.3(b) applies.
- D: That limit, in Rule 7.3(c)(1), applies to all solicitation; live person-to-person solicitation for gain is barred under Rule 7.3(b) regardless.
- E: Correct. Rule 7.3(b) forbids live person-to-person contact to solicit professional employment when a significant motive is pecuniary gain, unless the person contacted is a lawyer, has a family, close personal or prior business or professional relationship with the lawyer, or routinely uses the type of legal services offered for business purposes. Her roommate has a close personal relationship; the strangers don't.
Rule: Rule 7.3(b) bars live person-to-person solicitation for pecuniary gain except of (1) lawyers, (2) family, close personal, or prior business or professional contacts, or (3) routine business users of the services; Rule 7.3(c) bars any solicitation of people who have said no or that involves coercion, duress or harassment.

## Final 1 · Q89 · Advertising and Solicitation (MR 7.1–7.3, 7.6) — MR 7.1: misleading claims about results
Lawyer Jax's website says, truthfully, "We won $4 million for an injured worker last year." It doesn't mention that the case involved unusual facts and that most of the firm's cases settle for far less. Under the Model Rules, is the statement likely to be misleading?

A. No, because a statement that is literally true can never violate Rule 7.1.
B. No, because Bates and Zauderer give lawyers an absolute First Amendment right to advertise.
C. Yes, because lawyers may never mention past results in advertising.
D. Yes, because it may create unjustified expectations about results.
E. Yes, because any ad that mentions a dollar amount violates Rule 7.2.

Answer: D
- A: Rule 7.1 reaches truthful statements that are misleading because they omit necessary facts or create unjustified expectations.
- B: Bates and Zauderer protect truthful, non-misleading lawyer advertising; states may still regulate misleading ads.
- C: Too broad. Past results may be mentioned if not misleading; Rule 7.1, Comment [3] suggests qualifying language can prevent unjustified expectations.
- D: Correct. Rule 7.1 forbids false or misleading communications, including truthful statements that omit facts needed to keep them from being misleading. Rule 7.1, Comment [3] says a truthful report of a lawyer's achievements on behalf of clients may be misleading if presented so as to lead a reasonable person to form an unjustified expectation; a disclaimer or qualifying language may cure it.
- E: Rule 7.2 governs advertising mechanics, such as payment for recommendations and required contact information; it doesn't ban dollar figures.
Rule: Rule 7.1 bars false or misleading communications about a lawyer's services, including truthful statements that omit facts or create unjustified expectations (Comment [3]); qualifying language may cure the risk, and Zauderer allows required disclosures to prevent deception.

## Final 1 · Q90 · Avoiding Invidious Discrimination (MR 8.4(g)) — MR 8.4(g): conduct related to the practice of law
At a law firm's holiday party for its lawyers and staff, Partner Kip repeatedly makes demeaning jokes about a junior associate's national origin, after she asks him to stop. The firm says the party was a social event, not law practice. Is Kip subject to discipline under Rule 8.4(g)?

A. No, because a firm party is a social event, not the practice of law.
B. Yes, because harassment at a firm social event is conduct related to the practice of law.
C. No, because the First Amendment protects jokes, however offensive.
D. No, unless the associate files an employment discrimination claim against the firm.
E. Yes, but only because Kip, as a partner, is responsible for the firm's workplace under Rule 5.1.

Answer: B
- A: Rule 8.4, Comment [4] expressly reaches social activities in connection with the practice of law, such as a firm party.
- B: Correct. Rule 8.4(g) forbids conduct the lawyer knows or reasonably should know is harassment or discrimination on the basis of, among other things, national origin, in conduct related to the practice of law. Rule 8.4, Comment [4] includes interacting with coworkers and participating in business or social activities in connection with the practice of law, and Comment [3] defines harassment to include derogatory or demeaning verbal conduct.
- C: Burk notes the First Amendment debate over Rule 8.4(g), but under the Model Rule as written, demeaning harassment of a coworker at a firm event is covered.
- D: Discipline under Rule 8.4(g) doesn't depend on a civil claim; Comment [3] says substantive antidiscrimination law may guide but doesn't limit it.
- E: Kip's own conduct violates Rule 8.4(g); his responsibility doesn't depend on his management role.
Rule: Rule 8.4(g) bars conduct the lawyer knows or reasonably should know is harassment or discrimination on listed bases in conduct related to the practice of law, which Comment [4] defines to include dealings with coworkers and firm social events; it doesn't limit accepting, declining or withdrawing under Rule 1.16 or legitimate advocacy.

## Final 2 · Q1 · Sources of Law and the Model Rules — Which rules bind: state adoption of the Model Rules
Lawyer Dara, admitted only in Delaware, is charged by Delaware's disciplinary counsel with violating a rule. Dara argues that the ABA Model Rules can't bind her, because the ABA is a private association she never joined. Which statement best describes the law?

A. Dara is bound by the ABA Model Rules directly, because every American lawyer is subject to them.
B. Dara is bound only by rules the state legislature enacted, because only legislatures can regulate a profession.
C. Dara is bound by the rules her state's supreme court adopted, which are largely based on the Model Rules.
D. Dara is bound by no ethics rules unless she voluntarily joined the state bar association.
E. Dara is bound by the ABA Model Rules only in federal court, and by state rules everywhere else.

Answer: C
- A: The ABA has no regulatory power. The Model Rules matter only as adopted by a state's court, as Rule 8.5(a) assumes when it speaks of each jurisdiction's own rules.
- B: In most states the judiciary, not the legislature, regulates admission and discipline of lawyers through its inherent power over the bar.
- C: Correct. The ABA Model Rules are a model; they bind no one on their own. Each state's highest court adopts its own rules of professional conduct (usually based on the Model Rules, sometimes with changes), and those adopted rules are what the state's disciplinary system enforces, as Burk Ch. 3.A explains.
- D: Admission to practice, not membership in a voluntary bar association, subjects a lawyer to the state's rules and disciplinary authority (Rule 8.5(a)).
- E: Federal courts adopt their own rules, often borrowing state rules; the ABA text isn't automatically binding anywhere.
Rule: The Model Rules are a model code; a lawyer is bound by the rules her jurisdiction's high court has adopted (often the Model Rules with variations), and Rule 8.5 governs which jurisdiction's rules apply.

## Final 2 · Q2 · Bar Admission and Discipline (MR 8.1, 8.2, 8.4) — MR 8.1(b): responding to disciplinary counsel
Disciplinary counsel writes to Lawyer Hank asking for his trust-account records in an investigation of a client's complaint. Hank believes the complaint is baseless and throws the letter away without responding. Two follow-up letters go unanswered too. The records contain no information Hank's clients have asked him to keep confidential. Is Hank subject to discipline for failing to respond?

A. No, because he can't be disciplined unless the client's underlying complaint is proved.
B. No, because the Fifth Amendment lets a lawyer refuse to cooperate in a disciplinary investigation.
C. Yes, because ignoring a lawful demand from disciplinary counsel is itself misconduct.
D. Yes, but only if disciplinary counsel first obtains a subpoena for the records.
E. No, because Rule 8.1 governs only statements made in bar admission applications.

Answer: C
- A: Failing to respond is an independent violation of Rule 8.1(b), whatever happens to the original complaint.
- B: Rule 8.1, Comment [2] says a lawyer may assert a constitutional privilege openly, but Hank simply ignored the demand, which is what Rule 8.1(b) forbids.
- C: Correct. Rule 8.1(b) makes it misconduct to "knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand for information from an admissions or disciplinary authority," except that it doesn't require disclosure of information protected by Rule 1.6. Ignoring the inquiry is a separate violation even if the underlying complaint fails.
- D: Rule 8.1(b) applies to a "lawful demand for information"; a subpoena isn't a prerequisite.
- E: Rule 8.1 covers both bar admission applications and disciplinary matters.
Rule: Rule 8.1 forbids, in bar admission and disciplinary matters, (a) knowing false statements of material fact and (b) failing to correct a known misapprehension or knowingly failing to respond to a lawful demand for information, subject to Rule 1.6.

## Final 2 · Q3 · Bar Admission and Discipline (MR 8.1, 8.2, 8.4) — Bradwell v. The State
In Bradwell v. The State (1873), the Supreme Court considered Illinois's refusal to admit Myra Bradwell to its bar because she was a married woman. Which statement best describes the decision and why the course studies it?

A. The Court ordered her admission, holding that the Fourteenth Amendment forbids excluding women from the bar.
B. The Court held that Congress, not the states, controls who may practice law in state courts.
C. The Court upheld the refusal, holding that admission to a state bar is for the state to regulate.
D. The Court upheld the refusal because Bradwell had failed the Illinois bar examination.
E. The Court dismissed the case as moot after Illinois changed its rules to admit women.

Answer: C
- A: The Court ruled the other way; it rejected her Fourteenth Amendment claim.
- B: Bradwell treated admission to a state's bar as a matter for the state.
- C: Correct. In Bradwell the Court held that the right to practice law in a state's courts is not a privilege or immunity of national citizenship protected by the Fourteenth Amendment, so Illinois could exclude her. A concurrence invoked women's supposed "proper" domestic sphere, which is why the course reads it as an example of how bar regulation was used to exclude, and of the dangers of regulating "character" and fitness.
- D: Her qualifications weren't the issue; she was excluded because she was a married woman.
- E: The Court decided the merits and upheld the exclusion.
Rule: Bradwell (1873) upheld Illinois's exclusion of a woman from the bar, holding that practicing law in state courts isn't a privilege of national citizenship; it shows states' broad power over bar admission and how that power was used to exclude.

## Final 2 · Q4 · Where You May Practice (MR 5.5, 8.5) — MR 5.5(d)(2): services authorized by federal law
Lawyer Imani is admitted only in New York. She opens an office in New Jersey and practices exclusively federal immigration law, representing clients before federal immigration agencies and immigration courts. Her letterhead and website state that she is admitted only in New York and that her practice is limited to federal immigration matters. Is Imani engaged in the unauthorized practice of law in New Jersey?

A. Yes, because Rule 5.5(b) forbids any office in a state where the lawyer isn't admitted.
B. No, because Rule 5.5(c) lets any lawyer practice in another state on a temporary basis.
C. Yes, unless she associates with a New Jersey lawyer who actively participates in each matter.
D. No, because federal law authorizes that practice and she discloses her limits.
E. No, because a lawyer may practice anywhere once she discloses where she is admitted.

Answer: D
- A: Rule 5.5(b) is subject to Rule 5.5(d), which allows a systematic presence to provide services authorized by federal law.
- B: An office is not temporary. Imani is protected by Rule 5.5(d)(2), not the temporary-practice safe harbors of Rule 5.5(c).
- C: Association with local counsel is a Rule 5.5(c)(1) safe harbor for temporary work; Imani's federal practice needs none.
- D: Correct. Rule 5.5(d)(2) lets a lawyer admitted elsewhere provide in a jurisdiction "services that the lawyer is authorized by federal or other law or rule to provide," even through a systematic and continuous presence (Rule 5.5, Comment [18]). Federal law authorizes lawyers admitted in any state to appear before immigration agencies. Rule 5.5(b)(2) also bars holding herself out as admitted in New Jersey, and her disclosures avoid that.
- E: Disclosure alone doesn't authorize practice; the authorization here comes from federal law under Rule 5.5(d)(2).
Rule: Rule 5.5(d) allows a lawyer admitted elsewhere to have a systematic presence in a jurisdiction to (1) serve her employer as in-house counsel or (2) provide services federal or other law authorizes; she must not hold herself out as admitted there (Rule 5.5(b)(2)).

## Final 2 · Q5 · Where You May Practice (MR 5.5, 8.5) — MR 5.5(a): assisting unauthorized practice
Lawyer Kofi lets his experienced paralegal, Lars, meet alone with walk-in clients, tell them whether they have good claims, and quote them settlement values. Kofi rarely reviews what Lars tells clients. Is Kofi subject to discipline?

A. No, because paralegals may give legal advice so long as they work for a licensed lawyer.
B. No, because only Lars, who gave the advice, has engaged in the unauthorized practice of law.
C. Yes, but only if a client is harmed by advice Lars gave.
D. Yes, because he is assisting a nonlawyer in the unauthorized practice of law.
E. No, because quoting settlement values is business advice, not the practice of law.

Answer: D
- A: Working for a lawyer doesn't authorize a nonlawyer to advise clients; the work must be supervised and the lawyer must remain responsible (Rule 5.5, Comment [2]).
- B: Rule 5.5(a) separately forbids assisting another in unauthorized practice, so Kofi is responsible too.
- C: Discipline for assisting unauthorized practice doesn't depend on harm to a client.
- D: Correct. Rule 5.5(a) forbids a lawyer to "assist another in doing so," meaning practicing law in violation of the jurisdiction's regulation of the profession. Rule 5.5, Comment [2] lets lawyers delegate work to paraprofessionals only if the lawyer supervises the delegated work and retains responsibility for it. Evaluating claims for clients without supervision is practicing law. Rule 5.3 is violated too.
- E: Telling a person whether she has a good legal claim and what it is worth is legal advice, a core part of practicing law.
Rule: Rule 5.5(a) forbids practicing law where not authorized or assisting another to do so; lawyers may delegate to nonlawyers only with supervision and retained responsibility (Comment [2]; Rule 5.3).

## Final 2 · Q6 · Consequences: Civil Liability, Sanctions, and Other Law — Sanctions for AI-fabricated citations (Mata)
Lawyer Nils uses a generative AI tool to draft a brief, and files it without checking the cases it cites. Several cases turn out not to exist. When the court asks, Nils at first insists the cases are real. Which statement best describes Nils's exposure?

A. He faces no consequences, because he didn't know the cases were fake when he filed the brief.
B. He may be disciplined, but a court has no power to sanction a lawyer for the contents of a brief.
C. He may be sanctioned only if the opposing party lost money because of the fake citations.
D. He is protected, because the AI vendor, not the lawyer, is responsible for the content it produces.
E. He may be sanctioned by the court and also disciplined, as in Mata v. Avianca.

Answer: E
- A: A lawyer must make a reasonable inquiry before filing (FRCP 11(b)), and Nils doubled down once the problem was raised.
- B: Courts may sanction filings under FRCP 11 and their inherent power, as Mata v. Avianca shows.
- C: Rule 11 sanctions don't require proof of the opponent's financial loss; they deter baseless filings.
- D: The lawyer who signs a filing is responsible for it; using a tool is like using a nonlawyer assistant, whose work the lawyer must supervise (Rule 5.3).
- E: Correct. In Mata v. Avianca the court imposed Rule 11 sanctions on lawyers who filed AI-fabricated citations and then stood by them. The same conduct can violate Rule 1.1 (competence, including understanding technology), Rule 3.3(a)(1) (false statements to a tribunal) and Rule 8.4(c). Court sanctions and discipline are separate consequences.
Rule: A lawyer who files fabricated or unchecked citations risks court sanctions (FRCP 11, inherent power; Mata) and discipline under Rules 1.1, 3.3(a)(1) and 8.4(c); the consequences stack.

## Final 2 · Q7 · Consequences: Civil Liability, Sanctions, and Other Law — Malpractice causation: the case within a case
Lawyer Opal missed the statute of limitations on Client Ray's claim against a contractor, so the claim was dismissed. Ray sues Opal for malpractice. Opal concedes she was negligent. What must Ray ordinarily prove to recover damages?

A. Nothing more, because a conceded breach of duty establishes the lawyer's liability for the lost claim.
B. That Opal violated Rule 1.3, because a disciplinary violation is what makes a lawyer liable in damages.
C. That Opal intended to let the deadline pass.
D. That he would have obtained a better result on the underlying claim but for her negligence.
E. That Opal has been disciplined by the state bar for the missed deadline.

Answer: D
- A: Breach is only one element; Ray must also prove causation and damages.
- B: The Scope says a Rule violation doesn't itself create a cause of action. Malpractice is proved by duty, breach, causation and damages.
- C: Malpractice is ordinarily negligence; intent isn't required.
- D: Correct. Burk Ch. 3.B describes causation in malpractice as the "case within a case": the client must show that, absent the lawyer's error, he would have won (or done better on) the underlying claim, and that the judgment would have been collectible.
- E: A disciplinary finding isn't an element of a civil malpractice claim.
Rule: Legal malpractice requires (all required) (1) a duty (usually from a client-lawyer relationship), (2) breach of the standard of care, (3) causation, proved by showing the better result the client would have obtained (the "case within a case"), and (4) damages.

## Final 2 · Q8 · Why Smart People Do Stupid Things (Ch. 4) — MR 1.16(a)(2): impairment
Lawyer Pell has been drinking heavily during a hard divorce. He has missed two court dates and can no longer keep track of his cases. He hasn't sought help and keeps taking new matters. Which statement about Pell's obligations is correct?

A. He may keep all his cases so long as no client has yet been harmed.
B. He must withdraw from matters his condition materially impairs his ability to handle, and should get help.
C. He must close his practice permanently, because an impaired lawyer may not practice law.
D. He must report himself to the disciplinary authority under Rule 8.3 before doing anything else.
E. He may keep his cases if he has a paralegal handle the court appearances he can't attend.

Answer: B
- A: Rule 1.16(a)(2) turns on material impairment of his ability to represent, not on whether harm has already occurred.
- B: Correct. Rule 1.16(a)(2) requires withdrawal when "the lawyer's physical or mental condition materially impairs the lawyer's ability to represent the client." Burk Ch. 4 stresses that lawyers under stress should get help, such as a lawyer assistance program, before the impairment produces misconduct.
- C: The Rules require withdrawal from matters he can't handle, not a permanent end to practice; impairment can be treated.
- D: Rule 8.3 concerns reporting another lawyer's misconduct; it doesn't require self-reporting.
- E: A nonlawyer can't appear for a client in court, and delegating doesn't cure the impairment of the responsible lawyer.
Rule: Under Rule 1.16(a)(2) a lawyer must withdraw when his physical or mental condition materially impairs his ability to represent the client; Burk Ch. 4 urges getting help early, through lawyer assistance programs among others.

## Final 2 · Q9 · Key Definitions (MR 1.0) — MR 1.0(f): knowledge inferred from circumstances
Lawyer Quinn's client, a defendant in a car-accident case, plans to testify that he was driving at 30 mph. Quinn has seen the crash-reconstruction report, the client's own text sent minutes after the crash saying "I was doing 70," and dashcam video showing high speed. Quinn tells himself he doesn't really "know" the testimony is false. Under the Model Rules, does Quinn know?

A. No, because "knows" requires the client to admit to the lawyer that the testimony is false.
B. No, because a lawyer is entitled to resolve all doubts in the client's favor.
C. Yes, because he reasonably should know the testimony is false, which is the same as knowing.
D. Yes, but only if a court has already ruled that the client's speed was 70 mph.
E. He may be found to know, because knowledge may be inferred from circumstances.

Answer: E
- A: An admission is the clearest proof, but Rule 1.0(f) lets knowledge be inferred from circumstances.
- B: Rule 3.3, Comment [8] lets a lawyer resolve doubts in the client's favor, but not to ignore an obvious falsehood.
- C: "Reasonably should know" (Rule 1.0(j)) is a different, objective standard; Rule 3.3(a)(3) uses "knows," which here may be inferred from the circumstances.
- D: Knowledge under Rule 1.0(f) doesn't depend on a court's finding.
- E: Correct. Rule 1.0(f) defines "knows" as actual knowledge of the fact, but adds that "a person's knowledge may be inferred from circumstances." Rule 3.3, Comment [8] says a lawyer cannot ignore an obvious falsehood. With the text, the video and the report, a factfinder may infer that Quinn knows.
Rule: "Knows" (Rule 1.0(f)) means actual knowledge, which may be inferred from circumstances; it differs from "reasonably should know" (Rule 1.0(j)), and a lawyer can't ignore an obvious falsehood (Rule 3.3, Comment [8]).

## Final 2 · Q10 · Competence and Diligence (MR 1.1, 1.3) — MR 1.3, Comment [2]: controlling workload
Lawyer Rina takes on so many cases that she routinely files motions at the last minute and twice asks for extensions because she hasn't started a brief. No client has lost a case or a claim because of the delays. Is Rina subject to discipline?

A. No, because no client has suffered any harm from the delays.
B. Yes, because her chronic delays breach the duty of diligence.
C. No, because extensions are a normal part of litigation that courts routinely grant.
D. Yes, but only if a client files a malpractice suit.
E. No, because diligence is a question of malpractice law, not of professional discipline.

Answer: B
- A: Rule 1.3 isn't limited to delays that cause substantive harm; Comment [3] recognizes that unreasonable delay itself injures clients.
- B: Correct. Rule 1.3 requires "reasonable diligence and promptness," and Rule 1.3, Comment [2] says a lawyer's workload must be controlled so that each matter can be handled competently. Comment [3] notes that delay can cause clients needless anxiety and undermine confidence even when the client's interests aren't harmed in substance.
- C: Occasional extensions are fine; chronic delay from an unmanageable workload violates Rule 1.3.
- D: Discipline under Rule 1.3 doesn't depend on a civil suit.
- E: Rule 1.3 is a disciplinary rule, separate from the civil standard of care.
Rule: Rule 1.3 requires reasonable diligence and promptness; Comment [2] requires controlling workload, Comment [3] warns that procrastination harms clients even without substantive loss, and Comment [5] urges a sole practitioner to plan for death or disability.

## Final 2 · Q11 · The Civil Duty of Care and Effective Assistance — Roe v. Flores-Ortega: the lost appeal
After sentencing, Defendant Sam tells his appointed lawyer, Tia, "I want to appeal." Tia thinks an appeal is hopeless and never files a notice of appeal, and the deadline passes. Sam later seeks relief for ineffective assistance. Must Sam show that his appeal would likely have succeeded?

A. Yes, because Strickland always requires a reasonable probability of a different outcome.
B. Yes, because an appointed lawyer may decline to file an appeal she believes is frivolous.
C. No, because any failure to consult a client is presumptively prejudicial under United States v. Cronic.
D. Yes, unless the trial judge advised Sam of his right to appeal at sentencing.
E. No, because a lawyer who disregards an instruction to appeal is deficient, and prejudice is presumed.

Answer: E
- A: Flores-Ortega adapts Strickland: when counsel's error forfeits the appeal itself, the defendant need show only that he would have appealed.
- B: A lawyer who thinks an appeal frivolous may follow procedures for withdrawing, but she may not simply ignore the client's instruction to appeal.
- C: Cronic covers the complete breakdown of the adversarial process; Flores-Ortega is the rule for a lost appeal.
- D: Sam told his lawyer to appeal; the judge's advice doesn't excuse counsel's failure to follow that instruction.
- E: Correct. In Roe v. Flores-Ortega the Court held that a lawyer who disregards a defendant's specific instruction to file a notice of appeal acts in a professionally unreasonable way, and that the defendant shows prejudice by showing he would have appealed, without showing the appeal had merit. Whether to appeal is the client's decision (Rule 1.2(a)).
Rule: Roe v. Flores-Ortega: disregarding a client's instruction to appeal is deficient performance, and prejudice is shown by proof that the defendant would have appealed; the decision to appeal belongs to the client (Rule 1.2(a)).

## Final 2 · Q12 · Forming the Relationship and Identifying the Client — Declining a representation
A wealthy businessman, Tom, asks Lawyer Uma to represent his company in a commercial lease dispute. Uma declines, explaining politely that she disagrees with his public political views and prefers not to work with him. Tom complains to the bar. Is Uma subject to discipline?

A. Yes, because a lawyer must accept any client who can pay a reasonable fee.
B. No, because a lawyer may generally decline a private matter for reasons like hers.
C. Yes, because declining a client for his political views is discrimination under Rule 8.4(g).
D. No, but only because Tom's company is an organization rather than an individual.
E. Yes, unless Uma refers Tom to another lawyer who will take the case.

Answer: B
- A: No rule requires a lawyer to accept every paying client; the profession's ideals (Rule 6.1) are aspirational.
- B: Correct. Apart from court appointments (Rule 6.2), lawyers generally aren't obliged to accept any particular client. Rule 8.4(g) expressly "does not limit the ability of a lawyer to accept, decline or withdraw from a representation in accordance with Rule 1.16," and political views aren't among its protected categories.
- C: Political views aren't a protected category in Rule 8.4(g), and the rule expressly preserves the lawyer's ability to decline under Rule 1.16.
- D: Uma's freedom to decline doesn't depend on whether the prospective client is an organization.
- E: A referral is courteous but not required when declining a private matter.
Rule: Lawyers generally may decline private matters for almost any reason (subject to antidiscrimination law), but must accept court appointments absent good cause (Rule 6.2); Rule 8.4(g) doesn't limit accepting or declining under Rule 1.16.

## Final 2 · Q13 · Forming the Relationship and Identifying the Client — Identifying the client: insurance defense
An insurer hires Lawyer Val to defend its insured, Wade, in a car-accident suit. The insurer instructs Val not to file a motion that Val believes is in Wade's interest because the motion would be costly. Which statement best describes Val's duties?

A. Val must follow the insurer's instructions, because the insurer is paying for the defense.
B. Val must use independent judgment for Wade, and the insurer can't direct her otherwise.
C. Val represents only the insurer, so Wade's interests are irrelevant to her decision.
D. Val must withdraw at once, because insurance defense always creates a nonconsentable conflict.
E. Val may file the motion and bill Wade personally for it without telling the insurer.

Answer: B
- A: Payment doesn't give the insurer control of Val's professional judgment; Rule 5.4(c) and Rule 1.8(f) forbid it.
- B: Correct. Wade is Val's client (in many states the insurer is a client too). Rule 1.8(f) lets a third party pay only if there is no interference with the lawyer's independent judgment, and Rule 5.4(c) bars a payor from directing or regulating that judgment. If the insurer's limits conflict with Wade's interests, Val must address the conflict, not simply follow orders.
- C: Val was hired to defend Wade, who is at least a client; she owes him the full duties of the relationship.
- D: Insurance defense is routine; conflicts that arise can usually be managed or consented to under Rule 1.7.
- E: Hiding the decision from the payor and billing the client unilaterally raises Rule 1.4 and Rule 1.5 problems; the issue is resolved by communication, not concealment.
Rule: When a third party pays (insurance defense), the lawyer must identify the client, keep independent judgment (Rule 1.8(f), Rule 5.4(c)) and protect the client's information; a payor's instructions can't override the client's interests.

## Final 2 · Q14 · Scope of the Engagement and Duties to Non-Clients — Duty to a non-client invited to rely
At her client's request, Lawyer Xena writes a letter to Yale Bank, which is considering a loan to the client, stating that the client holds clear title to a warehouse. Xena never checked the title records, and the title is in fact encumbered. The bank relies on the letter and loses money. The bank was never Xena's client. Is Xena likely liable to the bank?

A. Yes, because she invited the bank to rely on her work and failed to use reasonable care.
B. No, because a lawyer owes duties only to her own clients.
C. No, because the bank should have hired its own lawyer to check the title.
D. Yes, but only if Xena knew the title was encumbered.
E. No, because Rule 2.3 says that evaluations for third persons never create duties to them.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. Burk Ch. 9.B explains that a lawyer can owe a duty of care to a non-client when the lawyer (or the client, with the lawyer's acquiescence) invites the non-client to rely on the lawyer's opinion or work, as with an opinion letter. Rule 2.3 also governs evaluations prepared for third persons.
- B: Privity is not always required; a non-client invited to rely on the lawyer's work can sue for negligent misrepresentation.
- C: The bank's choice not to hire its own lawyer doesn't defeat its reasonable reliance on an opinion addressed to it.
- D: Knowledge would add fraud, but negligence suffices for liability to an invited non-client.
- E: Rule 2.3 governs when a lawyer may give an evaluation; it doesn't immunize a careless one from civil liability.
Rule: Lawyers can owe non-clients a duty of care when they invite reliance, as with opinion letters to lenders, and to intended beneficiaries of their work; Rule 2.3 governs evaluations for third persons.

## Final 2 · Q15 · Scope of the Engagement and Duties to Non-Clients — Limited scope and the duty to warn: Nichols
Lawyer Zeke agrees to handle only Client Ava's workers' compensation claim for an on-the-job injury caused by a defective machine. He never tells her that she may also have a product-liability claim against the machine's manufacturer, or that he won't be handling it. The limitations period on that claim runs. Is Zeke likely liable to Ava?

A. Yes, because he should have warned her about the related claim he wasn't handling.
B. No, because he agreed only to handle the workers' compensation claim.
C. No, because the product claim was against a different defendant.
D. Yes, because a lawyer must pursue every claim a client may have, whatever the agreed scope.
E. No, because only a written engagement letter can create a duty to advise about other claims.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. In Nichols v. Keller, the court held that a lawyer who limits his representation to one claim may be liable for failing to advise the client of reasonably apparent related claims outside the engagement, or at least to tell her to get other advice. Rule 1.2(c) also requires that a limitation be reasonable and that the client give informed consent.
- B: An agreed limit on scope doesn't relieve the lawyer of the duty to alert the client to apparent related claims (Nichols).
- C: A different defendant doesn't make the claim less apparent or relevant to the client's injury.
- D: Too broad. A lawyer may limit scope under Rule 1.2(c); he must explain the limits so the client can protect herself.
- E: The duty to warn arises from the relationship itself, not from the form of the engagement.
Rule: A lawyer may limit scope under Rule 1.2(c) only if reasonable and with informed consent; Nichols v. Keller shows the lawyer should flag apparent related claims outside the engagement and tell the client to seek other advice.

## Final 2 · Q16 · Clients with Decision-Making Limitations (MR 1.14) — MR 1.14(a): following the client's own decisions
Client Bess, 84, has mild memory problems but understands her finances and can explain her reasons. She asks Lawyer Cy to change her will to leave most of her estate to her church instead of her children. Cy thinks the change is unwise and that her children will be upset. What should Cy do?

A. Refuse to make the change unless Bess's children agree to it.
B. Seek a guardian for Bess, because an unwise decision shows she can't protect her own interests.
C. Draft the will but tell her children about the change so they can object.
D. Draft the will as Bess directs, after confirming she understands and is acting voluntarily.
E. Withdraw, because a lawyer may not represent a client with memory problems.

Answer: D
- A: The children aren't Cy's clients; Bess decides the objectives of her own estate plan (Rule 1.2(a)).
- B: Protective action under Rule 1.14(b) requires a reasonable belief that the client has decision-making limitations and is at risk of substantial harm; an unconventional but reasoned choice doesn't meet that test.
- C: Telling the children would reveal client information without consent or a Rule 1.14(c) basis, violating Rule 1.6(a).
- D: Correct. Rule 1.14(a) requires the lawyer to maintain an ordinary client-lawyer relationship as far as reasonably possible, which includes abiding by the client's decisions about objectives (Rule 1.14, Comment [4]). Decision-making limitations can be situational (Comment [2]); Bess can make this decision, and disagreement isn't grounds for protective action.
- E: Rule 1.14(a) directs the lawyer to keep the relationship as ordinary as possible, not to abandon a client with some limitations.
Rule: Rule 1.14(a): keep an ordinary relationship with a client with decision-making limitations as far as reasonably possible, including following her decisions (Comment [4]); protective action under Rule 1.14(b) needs a risk of substantial harm and an inability to act in her own interest.

## Final 2 · Q17 · Declining and Terminating the Representation (MR 1.16) — MR 1.16(a)(1): representation would violate the Rules
Client Dot insists that Lawyer Eli file a lawsuit against her neighbor that Eli has concluded has no factual or legal basis and is meant only to harass the neighbor into selling his house. Dot refuses to drop it. What must Eli do?

A. File the suit, because the decision to sue is the client's objective under Rule 1.2(a).
B. File the suit but tell the court that he believes it lacks merit.
C. Decline or withdraw, because the representation would result in a violation of the Rules.
D. Withdraw if he wishes, but he isn't required to, because the choice is permissive.
E. Report Dot to the disciplinary authority for proposing a frivolous suit.

Answer: C
- A: Clients set objectives, but a lawyer can't pursue them by means that violate the Rules, such as a frivolous suit (Rule 3.1).
- B: Filing it would still violate Rule 3.1 and Rule 4.4(a), and announcing his doubts would also breach his duties to Dot.
- C: Correct. Rule 1.16(a)(1) requires a lawyer to decline or withdraw if "the representation will result in violation of the Rules of Professional Conduct or other law." Filing a frivolous suit would violate Rule 3.1 and Rule 4.4(a).
- D: When the representation itself would violate the Rules, withdrawal is mandatory under Rule 1.16(a)(1), not merely permitted.
- E: Clients aren't subject to the Rules, and nothing requires reporting a client.
Rule: Rule 1.16(a) requires withdrawal if (1) the representation will violate the Rules or other law, (2) the lawyer's condition materially impairs him, (3) he is discharged, or (4) the client persists in using his services for a crime or fraud.

## Final 2 · Q18 · Declining and Terminating the Representation (MR 1.16) — MR 1.16(c), Comment [3]: confidentiality when seeking leave
Lawyer Fran must withdraw from a pending civil case because her client insists that she present evidence she knows is false. She files a motion for leave to withdraw. The judge asks why. What should Fran say?

A. That the client has asked her to present false evidence, because candor to the tribunal requires it.
B. Nothing at all, because a judge may not ask a lawyer why she wants to withdraw.
C. Whatever the client authorizes, and if he refuses, she must stay in the case.
D. The full facts in a sealed filing, because sealing removes any confidentiality concern.
E. That professional considerations require her to withdraw, without revealing the client's confidences.

Answer: E
- A: No false evidence has been offered, so Rule 3.3's remedial duty hasn't arisen; Comment [3] directs her to protect the client's confidences when seeking leave.
- B: Comment [3] recognizes that the court may ask; the answer is to cite professional considerations.
- C: She may properly seek withdrawal under Rule 1.16(a)(1) whatever the client wants; the question is how much to explain.
- D: Sealing reduces but doesn't eliminate the disclosure; Comment [3] says a statement of professional considerations ordinarily suffices.
- E: Correct. Rule 1.16, Comment [3] says the court may request an explanation, but the lawyer may be bound to keep the facts confidential, and "the lawyer's statement that professional considerations require termination of the representation ordinarily should be accepted as sufficient." Rule 1.16(c) still requires her to continue if the court orders it.
Rule: When seeking leave to withdraw, a lawyer should say that professional considerations require it and protect client confidences (Rule 1.16, Comment [3]); she must continue if the tribunal orders (Rule 1.16(c)).

## Final 2 · Q19 · Declining and Terminating the Representation (MR 1.16) — MR 1.16(b)(1): withdrawal without material adverse effect
Lawyer Gus is handling a routine trademark renewal for Client Hal. Early in the matter, before anything is due, Gus decides he no longer wants trademark work and tells Hal he is withdrawing. Gus helps Hal find a new lawyer and sends over the file. Hal is annoyed but not harmed. Was the withdrawal proper?

A. No, because a lawyer may withdraw only for one of the client-caused reasons listed in Rule 1.16(b).
B. No, because a lawyer must finish every matter he accepts unless the client consents to his leaving.
C. Yes, because the withdrawal caused no material adverse effect on the client.
D. Yes, but only because trademark renewal is too simple to require continuous representation.
E. No, because Gus must first obtain leave from the trademark office.

Answer: C
- A: Rule 1.16(b)(1) needs no reason at all; it turns only on the absence of material adverse effect.
- B: Client consent isn't required for permissive withdrawal under Rule 1.16(b).
- C: Correct. Rule 1.16(b)(1) permits withdrawal if "withdrawal can be accomplished without material adverse effect on the interests of the client," whatever the reason. Gus also met his Rule 1.16(d) duties by helping with new counsel and sending the file.
- D: The simplicity of the matter isn't the test; the test is whether withdrawal materially harms the client.
- E: Rule 1.16(c) applies only when applicable law requires a tribunal's permission; nothing suggests that here.
Rule: Rule 1.16(b) permits withdrawal on listed grounds, including (1) for any reason when it causes no material adverse effect; the lawyer must still meet Rule 1.16(c) and (d).

## Final 2 · Q20 · The Duty of Confidentiality (MR 1.6(a), (c)) — MR 1.6, Comment [4]: hypotheticals
At a continuing-education seminar, Lawyer Ike describes a tricky custody case he once handled, changing the names and the city and leaving out every detail that could identify the family. No one in the audience could figure out who the clients were. Is Ike subject to discipline?

A. Yes, because Rule 1.6 forbids discussing any information relating to a representation without consent.
B. No, because no listener could reasonably identify the client from his hypothetical.
C. No, because the custody case has ended, so the duty of confidentiality no longer applies.
D. Yes, unless Ike first obtained the clients' informed consent to use their case in teaching.
E. No, because statements at an educational seminar are privileged from discipline.

Answer: B
- A: Rule 1.6, Comment [4] permits properly disguised hypotheticals, because they don't reveal the client's information.
- B: Correct. Rule 1.6, Comment [4] says a lawyer's use of a hypothetical to discuss issues relating to the representation is permissible "so long as there is no reasonable likelihood that the listener will be able to ascertain the identity of the client or the situation involved."
- C: The duty survives the representation (Rule 1.9(c)); Ike is protected only because his hypothetical couldn't be traced to the client.
- D: Consent is one way to permit disclosure, but a properly anonymized hypothetical reveals nothing and needs no consent.
- E: There's no seminar privilege; the hypothetical is proper only because it doesn't identify the client.
Rule: Rule 1.6(a) covers all information relating to the representation, but Comment [4] permits hypotheticals when there is no reasonable likelihood the listener can identify the client or situation.

## Final 2 · Q21 · The Duty of Confidentiality (MR 1.6(a), (c)) — MR 1.6(a): information from third parties
While preparing Client Joy's defense in a fraud case, Lawyer Kit interviews a neighbor who mentions that Joy's brother has a gambling problem. Joy never told Kit this and it has nothing to do with the case. Kit later mentions the brother's gambling to a mutual acquaintance. Has Kit violated Rule 1.6?

A. No, because the information came from a neighbor, not from the client.
B. No, because the information concerns Joy's brother, who is not Kit's client.
C. Yes, because the duty covers information relating to the representation from any source.
D. No, because the information is unrelated to the legal issues in the fraud case.
E. Yes, but only because the information was embarrassing to Joy's family.

Answer: C
- A: The source doesn't matter; Rule 1.6, Comment [3] covers information from any source.
- B: Information about others that the lawyer learns in the representation is still "information relating to the representation."
- C: Correct. Rule 1.6, Comment [3] says confidentiality "applies not only to matters communicated in confidence by the client but also to all information relating to the representation, whatever its source." Kit learned this while working on Joy's case.
- D: "Relating to the representation" is broad; it includes information learned while representing the client, whether or not it bears on the legal issues.
- E: Rule 1.6(a) doesn't depend on whether the information is embarrassing; it protects all information relating to the representation.
Rule: The duty of confidentiality covers all information relating to the representation, whatever its source (Rule 1.6, Comment [3]); it is far broader than the attorney-client privilege.

## Final 2 · Q22 · Confidentiality, Privilege, and Work Product — Crime-fraud exception vs. the duty of confidentiality
Client Lou consulted Lawyer Mae about how to structure transfers to hide assets from creditors he intended to defraud. Mae refused to help. Lou's creditors later sue him and subpoena Mae to testify about the consultation. Which statement is correct?

A. The communications are privileged, because Mae refused to help and no fraud was committed through her.
B. The communications aren't privileged, so Mae may freely discuss them with anyone.
C. The communications are privileged, because a lawyer may never be compelled to testify about a client.
D. Likely not privileged under the crime-fraud exception, but Rule 1.6 still bars voluntary disclosure.
E. The communications are protected as opinion work product, which is never discoverable.

Answer: D
- A: The crime-fraud exception turns on the client's purpose in seeking advice, not on whether the lawyer helped.
- B: Losing the privilege doesn't end the duty of confidentiality; Rule 1.6(a) still governs voluntary disclosures.
- C: Privilege has exceptions, including crime-fraud, and Rule 1.6(b)(6) lets a lawyer comply with a court order.
- D: Correct. The attorney-client privilege doesn't protect communications made to further a future crime or fraud (the crime-fraud exception), so a court may compel Mae's testimony. The ethical duty in Rule 1.6(a) is separate: outside compelled testimony she still may not volunteer the information unless an exception applies, and Rule 1.6(b)(6) permits compliance with a court order.
- E: Work product protects materials prepared in anticipation of litigation, not a client's request for help with a fraud.
Rule: Privilege (evidence law) protects confidential lawyer-client communications for legal advice but excludes communications to further a crime or fraud; the Rule 1.6 duty is broader, applies outside court, and yields to a court order under Rule 1.6(b)(6).

## Final 2 · Q23 · Exceptions to Confidentiality (MR 1.6(b)) — MR 1.6(b)(4): seeking ethics advice
Lawyer Ned is unsure whether he must withdraw from a matter because of something his client told him. He calls Lawyer Ora, a former professor who teaches professional responsibility, describes the facts including some client confidences, and asks her advice. Is Ned subject to discipline?

A. Yes, because consulting another lawyer about a client's matter always requires the client's consent.
B. No, because Ora is a professor, not a practicing lawyer, so no disclosure occurred.
C. Yes, unless Ned first withdraws and the client becomes a former client.
D. No, because any conversation between two lawyers is privileged.
E. No, because he may reveal what's needed to get ethics advice about his own duties.

Answer: E
- A: Rule 1.6(b)(4) is an exception precisely so that a lawyer can seek ethics advice without the client's consent.
- B: Telling anyone is a disclosure; Ned is protected by the ethics-advice exception, not by Ora's job.
- C: Rule 1.6(b)(4) applies during the representation; no withdrawal is needed to seek advice.
- D: Conversations between lawyers aren't automatically privileged; the permission comes from Rule 1.6(b)(4).
- E: Correct. Rule 1.6(b)(4) permits disclosure "to secure legal advice about the lawyer's compliance with these Rules." Rule 1.6, Comment [9] explains that such consultation is often the best way to ensure compliance. Ned should still reveal no more than reasonably necessary.
Rule: Rule 1.6(b)(4) permits disclosure reasonably necessary to secure legal advice about the lawyer's own compliance with the Rules (Comment [9]).

## Final 2 · Q24 · Exceptions to Confidentiality (MR 1.6(b)) — MR 1.6(b)(6), Comment [15]: responding to a court order
A trial court orders Lawyer Pia to produce notes of her conversations with a former client in a dispute between the client and a third party. Pia believes the notes are privileged. Which course is proper?

A. Assert the privilege and object, and comply only if the order stands after review.
B. Produce the notes at once, because Rule 1.6(b)(6) permits disclosure required by a court order.
C. Refuse to produce the notes under any circumstances, even if held in contempt.
D. Destroy the notes so that they can't be produced.
E. Produce the notes but leave the client uninformed, because the client is a former client.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. Rule 1.6, Comment [15] says that absent the client's informed consent, the lawyer should assert on the client's behalf all nonfrivolous claims that the order isn't authorized or that the information is privileged, and consult the client about appeal. If review isn't sought or fails, Rule 1.6(b)(6) permits compliance with the order.
- B: Rule 1.6(b)(6) permits compliance eventually, but Comment [15] directs the lawyer first to assert the privilege and other nonfrivolous objections.
- C: After objections fail, Rule 1.6(b)(6) permits compliance; the Rules don't require defying a final order.
- D: Destroying material subject to a court order violates Rule 3.4(a) and is likely contempt.
- E: Comment [15] calls for consulting the client about appeal; Rule 1.9(c) continues to protect a former client's information.
Rule: When ordered to disclose, the lawyer should assert privilege and other nonfrivolous objections and consult the client about appeal (Rule 1.6, Comment [15]); then Rule 1.6(b)(6) permits compliance, limited to what is reasonably necessary.

## Final 2 · Q25 · Exceptions to Confidentiality (MR 1.6(b)) — MR 1.6(b)(2): preventing a future client fraud
Lawyer Quint has been drafting sale documents for Client Rex, a seller of used construction equipment. Quint learns that Rex has rolled back the hour meters on machines he is about to sell, using the sale documents Quint drafted, and that the buyer will lose hundreds of thousands of dollars. Rex refuses to stop. May Quint reveal the scheme to the buyer?

A. Yes, as far as necessary to prevent it, since Rex is using Quint's services.
B. No, because the disclosure exceptions in Rule 1.6(b) cover only threats to life and limb.
C. Yes, and he must, because a lawyer has a mandatory duty to prevent client fraud.
D. No, because the fraud hasn't yet been completed.
E. Yes, but only after Rex's buyer files a lawsuit against Rex.

Answer: A
- A: Correct. Rule 1.6(b)(2) permits disclosure "to prevent the client from committing a crime or fraud that is reasonably certain to result in substantial injury to the financial interests or property of another and in furtherance of which the client has used or is using the lawyer's services." Quint must also withdraw under Rule 1.16(a)(4) and stop assisting under Rule 1.2(d).
- B: Rule 1.6(b)(2) and (3) cover substantial financial injury from a client crime or fraud that uses the lawyer's services.
- C: Rule 1.6(b)(2) is permissive; disclosure is mandatory only in narrower settings such as Rule 3.3.
- D: Rule 1.6(b)(2) is designed for frauds not yet completed; it permits disclosure "to prevent" them.
- E: The purpose of Rule 1.6(b)(2) is prevention; waiting for a suit would defeat it.
Rule: Rule 1.6(b)(2) permits disclosure to prevent a client crime or fraud reasonably certain to cause substantial financial injury when the client is using or has used the lawyer's services; withdrawal is required under Rule 1.16(a)(4).

## Final 2 · Q26 · When Disclosure Becomes Mandatory; Hard Cases — The Lake Pleasant bodies case
Client Sol, charged with one murder, tells his lawyers in confidence that he also killed two missing hikers and describes where their bodies are. The hikers' parents publicly beg anyone with information to come forward. No one is in danger now. May the lawyers reveal the location of the bodies?

A. Yes, because the families' suffering is a substantial harm that the exceptions are designed to prevent.
B. No, because no exception covers past crimes when no one faces reasonably certain death or bodily harm.
C. Yes, because confidentiality never protects information about murders.
D. No, unless the lawyers first withdraw, after which they may disclose freely.
E. Yes, because the information isn't privileged, since the client confessed to a crime.

Answer: B
- A: Rule 1.6(b)(1) addresses death or substantial bodily harm to come, not the grief caused by a completed crime.
- B: Correct. This tracks the Lake Pleasant bodies case from the Week 3 handout. Rule 1.6(a) protects the information; Rule 1.6(b)(1) covers only preventing reasonably certain death or substantial bodily harm, and the financial-harm exceptions don't apply. The lawyers also may not move or hide the bodies (Rule 3.4(a)).
- C: There's no categorical exception for serious crimes; the exceptions in Rule 1.6(b) are specific and none fits.
- D: Withdrawal doesn't end the duty; Rule 1.9(c) protects former-client information too.
- E: A confession to past crimes is classic privileged communication, and Rule 1.6(a) is broader still.
Rule: Confidentiality protects even a client's confession of past crimes; Rule 1.6(b)(1) permits disclosure only to prevent reasonably certain future death or substantial bodily harm, and the lawyer must not conceal or tamper with evidence (Rule 3.4(a)).

## Final 2 · Q27 · The Lawyer as Fiduciary (Ch. 5) — The four fiduciary duties
Burk describes the lawyer as a fiduciary who owes the client four distinct duties, to be analyzed separately. Which of the following is NOT one of the four?

A. The duty of loyalty, putting the client's interests in the engagement ahead of the lawyer's own.
B. The duty to obey all of the client's instructions about tactics and strategy.
C. The duty of care, providing competent and diligent representation.
D. The duty of confidentiality, protecting information relating to the representation.
E. The duty of candor, keeping the client informed and telling the client the truth.

Answer: B
- A: Loyalty is the first and central fiduciary duty (Meinhard), carried out by the conflict rules such as Rule 1.7.
- B: Correct. Burk's four fiduciary duties are loyalty, care (competence and diligence), confidentiality, and candor (communication). Obedience isn't on the list: the lawyer controls most means after consultation (Rule 1.2(a)) and must refuse instructions that would violate the law or the Rules (Rule 1.16(a)(1)).
- C: Care is one of the four, carried out by Rules 1.1 and 1.3 and by malpractice law.
- D: Confidentiality is one of the four, carried out by Rule 1.6.
- E: Candor is one of the four, carried out by Rule 1.4.
Rule: The lawyer's four fiduciary duties are loyalty, care, confidentiality and candor, each analyzed separately; the lawyer is an agent who follows the client's lawful objectives but controls most means after consulting (Rule 1.2(a)).

## Final 2 · Q28 · The Lawyer as Fiduciary (Ch. 5) — Loyalty: advice free of the lawyer's self-interest
Lawyer Tina represents Client Uri on a one-third contingent fee. The defense offers $90,000 early in the case. Tina believes the claim is worth at least $250,000 at trial, but she is short on cash and a quick $30,000 fee would help her. She advises Uri to take the offer, saying it's a good deal. Which statement best describes Tina's conduct?

A. She acted properly, because the decision to settle belonged to Uri, not to her.
B. She acted properly, because a contingent fee aligns the lawyer's interests with the client's.
C. She breached only her duty of care, because she misjudged the value of the case.
D. She acted properly so long as she told Uri the amount of her fee from the settlement.
E. She breached her duty of loyalty by letting her own financial interest shape her advice.

Answer: E
- A: The decision is Uri's under Rule 1.2(a), but he is entitled to advice untainted by her self-interest.
- B: Contingent fees can misalign incentives, as here, where an early settlement serves the lawyer's cash needs over the client's recovery.
- C: She didn't misjudge it; she believed it was worth more and advised otherwise for her own benefit, which is loyalty.
- D: Disclosing the fee amount doesn't cure advice slanted by the lawyer's undisclosed self-interest.
